xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: The end of compulsory national service in Britain in 1957 (for those born after Oct 1, 1939) and its complete abolition in November 1960 meant that young men in bands like The Quarrymen were exempt from military service. This freedom allowed members like John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940), and by implication, all four future Beatles, to continue pursuing music rather than being drafted. "And that meant that the young men in a new group called the Corrie men wouldn't have to worry about going into the army, so they kept at it."

xref.title: Peaceful Departure from Toronto (1964)
xref.body: The day after their chaotic concerts, just before noon on September 7, 1964, The Beatles headed back to the Toronto airport. The sun was shining, the crowd was considerably smaller than the previous day, and the mood was distinctly different. The band signed autographs, posed for photos, waved to their admirers, and then boarded their plane, marking the end of their first Toronto visit. "The sun was shining, and the crowd was considerably smaller. The mood was also different. This was the end."

xref.title: Contractual Dispute with Main Man (1972-1975)
xref.body: David Bowie wanted out of his contract with Tony DeFries' management company, Main Man, by the end of 1974, just two years into their relationship. Despite selling millions of albums, Bowie realized that most of the profits were not reaching him, suspecting that the new contract signed with Main Man at the end of September 1972 was "weird." On January 29, 1975, Bowie informed RCA, his record label, of his intention to split from DeFries, sparking a battle over who owned Bowie's next album.

xref.title: Killing Off Ziggy Stardust (1973)
xref.body: At the end of the 1973 Ziggy Stardust tour, Bowie announced to the audience that it would be "the last show that we'll ever do." While the public thought he was retiring, Bowie intended to retire the Ziggy persona to make way for a new one, Aladdin Sane. This willingness to "kill himself off" and constantly reinvent was admired by punks. "What he really meant though was that he was killing off Ziggy."

xref.title: Post-Beatles Collaboration with McCartney (1973)
xref.body: George Martin, who built and ran Air Studios in London, agreed to produce the recording sessions for Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. This marked a significant reunion, as it was the first time Martin had worked with a Beatle since the conclusion of the "Abbey Road" sessions in 1969. Martin later compelled the Bond producers to use McCartney's version as the title sequence. "Martin agreed to produce the sessions marking this as the first time since the end of the Abbey Road sessions that he got to work with a beetle."

xref.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
xref.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."

xref.body: On June 11, 1977, Joe Strummer and Topper Headon were in Newcastle. xref.title: Disastrous American Tour and Final Performance (1978)
xref.body: The Sex Pistols' American tour culminated in their final performance at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. The tour was marred by hostile audiences, Sid Vicious's extreme intoxication and altercations, Malcolm McLaren's difficult management, and deep internal animosity, all of which were captured in the film "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle." This show marked the last time the original lineup would perform together for nearly 18 years, and the final appearance with Sid Vicious before his death 13 months later. "It shows a band at the end of their rope and literally ready to blow apart."

xref.title: Jazz Coleman Quits for Apocalypse (1982)
xref.body: In February 1982, following a performance, singer Jazz Coleman announced his departure from Killing Joke and his intention to move to Iceland. He was convinced that the apocalypse was near and believed Iceland offered the safest refuge. This conviction stemmed from his deep fascination with the occult and a growing paranoia developed after investigating various conspiracy theories concerning the end of the world. Shortly after, guitarist Jordy Walker joined him in Iceland, seemingly persuaded by Coleman's apocalyptic reasoning. "After a gig, he announced he was quitting killing joke and moving to Iceland."

xref.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (1982)
xref.body: Joe Strummer, a key voice of the British punk explosion, inexplicably vanished on April 26, 1982, the night before The Clash was due to leave on a major tour, forcing the tour to be scrapped. He was gone for eight full weeks, showing up suddenly in mid-May 1982, offering various unconfirmed explanations like running the Paris marathon or helping a girlfriend's mother out of jail, leading to speculation about a publicity stunt or burnout; this vanishing act retrospectively marked the beginning of the end for the band. "Joe Strummer, one of the voices of the whole British punk explosion had inexplicably disappeared, vanished."

xref.title: Name Change to Radiohead (1991)
xref.body: After signing with EMI, the label expressed dissatisfaction with the name "On a Friday" and instructed the band to find a new one. Various suggestions were considered, including "Jude the Obscure" (deemed "too obscure" from the Thomas Hardy novel), "Music" (liked by Tom but rejected), and "Gravitates" (which "didn't have the right ring to it"). The definitive name, "Radiohead," was discovered when someone retrieved a 1986 Talking Heads album, "True Stories," from Tom York's DJ collection, which featured a song of the same name. The name change officially occurred at the end of 1991. "And so it came to pass that at the end of 1991, on a Friday, became known as Radiohead."

xref.title: 1992 Seattle Free Show Ticketing Dispute
xref.body: In May 1992, Pearl Jam planned a free show in Seattle for approximately 30,000 people and approached Ticketmaster to handle the ticketing, as city requirements mandated monitoring the crowd size. Ticketmaster quoted costs of $1 to $1.50 per ticket, which would amount to $45,000 for the band to absorb. Pearl Jam ultimately decided not to use Ticketmaster for this event, a decision that marked the beginning of their significant conflict with the ticketing giant. "In the end, for this particular show, Pearl Jam elected not to use ticket master, but the experience somehow left a bad taste in their mouth. And this was the beginning of a fight."

xref.title: Eccentric Behavior and Sunday Night Live Incident (1992)
xref.body: During the tour for "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," John Frusciante exhibited increasingly erratic behavior, including bringing his guitar to meals, chain-smoking, and shaving his head on a whim. He broke a significant band rule by bringing his girlfriend on the European leg of the tour. A pivotal moment occurred during the band's "Saturday Night Live" performance when Anthony Kiedis believed Frusciante sabotaged their set, particularly during "Under the Bridge," where his guitar playing was described as "woozy and weird," and he blasted his guitar and vocals dissonantly at the end. Kiedis suspected Frusciante was on heroin during the performance. "John was experimenting the way he would have if we'd been rehearsing the tune. Well, we weren't. We were on TV in front of millions of people."

xref.title: Intervention and Rome Suicide Attempt (1994)
xref.body: By the end of March 1994, Kurt Cobain's family, friends, and business associates were acutely aware of his troubles, especially after a previous suicide attempt at a hotel in Rome. On March 25th, 1994, his wife, Courtney Love, organized a five-hour intervention at their Seattle home with doctors, friends, bandmates (Chris Novoselic, Dave Grohl, Pat Smear), and members of Nirvana's management and legal team, in an attempt to compel him to address his problems. xref.title: "Her Majesty" - Accidental Hidden Track
xref.body: The inclusion of "Her Majesty" as a hidden track on "Abbey Road" was an unintended consequence of studio procedure. After Paul McCartney requested the song's removal, tape assistant John Kerlander snipped it out and spliced it to the end of the master tape with 20 seconds of blank tape, in accordance with Abbey Road's rules for edited material. A mastering engineer either overlooked or misread Kerlander's note, resulting in the song's presence on the final master, which the Beatles found "really cool" and decided to keep. "And so the first hidden track came to be as the result of an accident."

Another rejected title was "Verse Chorus Verse," which was also the original name of the song later known as "Sappy." The final title, *In Utero*, was derived from a poem written by Courtney Love. "In the end, the title In Yudero was chosen because everyone realized that I hate myself and I want to die could encourage people to do some dangerous things and perhaps result in some lawsuits."

xref.title: Aftermath of Toronto Stage Collapse
xref.body: The Toronto show was canceled, and Scott Johnson's death devastated everyone involved. The incident led to a prolonged and unresolved legal process, including investigations, lawsuits, counter-suits, charges against Live Nation, Optics Staging and Services, and engineer Dominic Caligari (all pleaded not guilty), two criminal trials, and a mistrial. As of the end of 2018, no one had been held accountable, and no inquest had been conducted. Scott Johnson's father, Ken Johnson, an expert in scaffolding health and safety, had "no doubt why the accident happened." "And then came the long, farcical train of investigations, lawsuits, counter-suits, charges, switch judges, legal bureaucracies, two criminal trials, and in the end, a mistrial that left everything unresolved."

xref.title: Catalyst for British Music Boom and British Invasion

The Beatles, after a few years, broke through, igniting the British music scene and subsequently leading the British Invasion of North America. "After a couple of years, the Beatles broke through.
